subject: Computer Networking
title: Tim Berners-Lee's Invention
description: A short lesson to help you apply Tim Berners-Lee's Invention.

hook.text: In 1989, a physicist at CERN wanted to share research papers. He invented the World Wide Web instead.

buildup.text: Tim Berners-Lee combined hypertext, TCP/IP, and DNS into one system: a web of linked documents.

discovery.text: He created HTML for pages, HTTP for transfer, and URLs for addresses. Three pillars of the web.

twist.text: CERN made the web free for everyone in 1993. No patents, no royalties. A gift to humanity.

climax.text: The first website described the web project itself. It still runs at info.cern.ch — the web's origin.

punchline.text: One physicist's idea to share papers became the modern web.

quiz.question: What three technologies did Tim Berners-Lee create for the web?

details.summary: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 at CERN, creating HTML for documents, HTTP for transfer, and URLs for addressing. He built the first web browser and server, then made the technology freely available, enabling the explosive growth of the web as an open platform.
details.whyItMatters: The decision to make the web open and free shaped the modern internet. Understanding its origins explains why the web is document-centric, link-based, and built on open standards anyone can use.
takeaways: Berners-Lee created HTML, HTTP, and URLs as a unified system
The first website went live in 1991 at CERN in Switzerland
Making the web freely available enabled its explosive adoption

faq.question: What problem did the World Wide Web solve?
faq.answer: CERN researchers needed to share documents across different computer systems. Berners-Lee combined hypertext with the internet to create a universal document system. Anyone with a browser could access any document via its URL, regardless of what computer hosted it.

faq.question: Why did Berners-Lee give the web away for free?
faq.answer: CERN released the web technology into the public domain in 1993. Berners-Lee believed the web's value came from being universal — a proprietary standard would have fragmented it into competing systems. This decision is considered one of the most consequential in technology history.
